title: Assemble a data-cleanup prompt
scenario: Your orders export has the usual damage: order_date mixes two date formats, region has 214 blanks, order_id contains 38 suspected duplicates, and amount mixes dot and comma as decimal separators. You need a cleanup plan you can run and verify — not a magic clean file.
task: Fill the fields to assemble a cleanup request with the mess, the target state, the safety rules and the checks — then compare with a strong example.

fields.label: The mess — each problem with its count
fields.placeholder: Mixed date formats in order_date (612 rows); 214 blanks in region; 38 suspected duplicate order_id; mixed decimal separators in amount…

fields.label: The target — what the cleaned sheet must look like
fields.placeholder: Typed columns, ISO dates, one decimal separator, nothing filled, duplicates listed not deleted…

fields.label: Safety rules — what the cleanup may never do
fields.placeholder: Never invent or impute values; missing becomes [MISSING]; list rows to change before applying…

fields.label: The check — how each step is verified
fields.placeholder: Every step ends with a count of affected rows and one spot-check against the original…

sampleSolution:
My orders export has these problems: order_date mixes two date formats across 612 rows; region has 214 blanks; order_id contains 38 suspected duplicates; amount mixes dot and comma as decimal separators.

Target state: typed columns with ISO dates (YYYY-MM-DD), one decimal separator, duplicates listed in a separate sheet rather than deleted, and no filled values anywhere.

Rules: never invent or impute a value — every missing value stays visible as [MISSING]; do not delete or merge duplicate rows, just report them with their row numbers; do not change anything I have not described.

Give me the cleanup as ordered passes, one change type per pass (dates → decimal separators → duplicates → types). For each pass: the exact transformation or formula, the count of rows it would affect, and one spot-check I can run to confirm the pass did what it claims. Finish with a before/after comparison plan: which totals I should expect to stay identical.
hints: Problems with counts turn vague cleaning into a testable plan — the counts are the specification.
The check field is where the cleanup stops being trust and becomes verification: counts, spot-checks, before/after totals.
explanation: The assembled prompt converts "clean this" into a verified process: the inventory with counts, a target state, a never-fill rule and a check per pass. Each pass is an isolated change with its own count — so when a total moves that should not have moved, the pass that caused it is findable in minutes instead of discovered in a meeting.
